To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a mutant of Haemphilus influenzae, which was completely unable (at physiological pH) to take up double stranded DNA, has a defect in the synthesis of one of its proteins, which is required for DNA binding.
the mutant was unable to take up DNA at normal physiological conditions (pH 7.0) but took up DNA equally well as the wild-type strain at low pH (4.4).

the DNA entry system of Haemophilous influenzae is composed of two distinct mechanisms and that the mutant is deficient in the synthesis of one of the proteins required for the entry mechanism operating at neutral pH.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mutant is defective in the synthesis of the competence protein P22.
in the mutant, which has a deficiency in DNA-binding proteins, the synthesis of a competence-specific membrane protein is also defective.

a protein with a specific base sequence requirement for DNA entry is synthesized during competence induction, and that this protein, in addition to its DNA entry function, is also involved in the regulation of the synthesis of a membrane protein with a molecular wt of 22,000 which is required for DNA entry at neutral pH.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mutant is unable to take up DNA at normal physiological conditions (pH 7.4) because it lacks the protein which recognizes the base sequence(s) in DNA required for entry.
the mutant provides a tool for the identification and characterization of the protein(s) involved in the entry of DNA into H. influenzae.
there are two different mechanisms for the entry of DNA in H. influenzae and that the mechanism which is responsible for entry at neutral pH requires the synthesis of a 22,500-dalton protein.
